https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cyvl.text: Image source, Reuters By Bethany Bell BBC correspondent ,Â Reporting from Leipzig Published 5 August 2026, 13:48 BST Updated 17 minutes ago A drone carrying an explosive device has been found at a German airport, police say. A robot was deployed at Leipzig/Halle Airport after the device was spotted in the cargo operation area overnight, according to Saxony police. A second unidentified object collided with a cargo aircraft near the same airport. Minor damage was detected on the aircraft after it landed in Hanover. There have been a series of unauthorised drone flights in Germany in recent months over sensitive sites including military bases, airports, energy terminals, seaports and logistics companies. German airports are on high alert. Federal police have warned that the overflights could have been organised by Russian agents. A police spokesman told the BBC that the object discovered at Leipzig Airport overnight had been spotted close to parked Ukrainian Antonov transport planes. The object was examined with the assistance of the Federal Police and an explosive-detection robot. The Federal Police's Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) unit removed the detonator from the explosive device. Flights on the northern runway resumed at 01:55 (23:55 GMT on Tuesday). The southern runway, which is a major hub for the logistic group DHL, remains closed. Saxony's Interior Minister Armin Schuster has described it as a "very serious security incident". In July 2024 a parcel burst into flames on the ground at Leipzig airport before it could be loaded onto a DHL cargo plane, one of a series of parcel fires that targeted the UK and EU countries. There are suspicions it could have been sabotage linked to Moscow. The parcels had contained explosive devices that were set off by electronic timers hidden in vibrating massage pillows, according to authorities. Russia has denied any involvement in those incidents. Last year a Chinese woman was convicted for passing on information about flight schedules and cargo movements at Leipzig-Halle Airport to a man spying for Beijing. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Displaced Yemenis at a shelter north of Aden in southern Yemen. Thousands have been forced to flee their homes as fighting in the country intensifies. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Yemen Houthis threaten more Saudi strikes as UN warns of humanitarian crisis in Yemen Estimated 100,000 Yemenis displaced amid renewed fighting as Qatar sounds alarm over Bab al-Mandab strait Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Tue 15 Sep 2026 13.25 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 14.54 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Saudi cities faced the threat of a second day of Houthi attacks as fighting across Yemen led the UN to warn of a humanitarian crisis with 100,000 Yemenis already displaced. As oil prices remained well over $100 (£74) a barrel, Qatar warned of a catastrophe if the Iran-backed Houthi militants won full control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea dominating the key naval route to Asia. The strait has become vital to Saudi crude oil exports as the wider Middle East war chokes the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. An emergency meeting of the UN security council in New York heard repeated calls for Houthi forces to show restraint. In a sign that Iran is still seeking a broader solution, its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, travelled to Beijing to discuss China’s possible role in solving the related strait of Hormuz dispute. The future of the strait of Hormuz – through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited in peacetime and which the US and Iran are now mounting blockades of – is the diplomatic key to unlocking the conflict between the US and Iran, and to a lesser extent the related conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. Oil prices rose sharply after Reuters reported that ⁠loadings at Saudi Arabia’s ⁠Red ⁠Sea port ​of Yanbu had ⁠been suspended, citing shipping industry sources. The price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose nearly 3% to $108 a barrel. Prices have risen this week after the ⁠world’s biggest ​crude ‌oil exporter, Saudi Aramco, ‌ closed its East-West ‌pipeline due to an attack by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. Aramco had increased ⁠use of the ​Yanbu terminal since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February. View image in fullscreen A screen grab from a Houthi video released earlier this week purporting to show militants on an armoured personnel carrier during an offensive near Yemen’s Red Sea city of Mocha. Photograph: Houthi Military Media Center Handout/EPA Qatar, acting as a mediator in the Iran war, is still trying to revive a postponed meeting planned for Monday between Iran and most Gulf Cooperation Council countries. The planned talks in Oman were delayed at the insistence of Saudi Arabia in protest at what it regarded as Iranian-inspired Houthi attacks on Saudi cities. The Houthis had claimed responsibility for a new “large-scale” attack using “dozens of ballistic missiles and drones” against King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait , southern Saudi Arabia, on Monday. Air raid sirens were activated in six governorates including Jeddah on Tuesday. The warnings were lifted relatively quickly, but reflect an unprecedented new state of insecurity across Saudi Arabia. The Oman meeting had been organised with the intention of reaching a regional agreement on an authorised route for commercial shipping through the strait of Hormuz. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, spoke with Oman’s foreign minister , Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, on Tuesday amid US concern that Oman will cede excessive control of the waterway to Iran. View image in fullscreen A shipping vessel anchored off Yemen’s coast in the Bab al-Mandab strait. Qatar has warned a blockade of the waterway could have a significant impact on world trade. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images The prospect of the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab straits both being under the long-term control of anti-western forces would be a significant strategic reversal for the US and Europe. The Qatar foreign ministry official Ibrahim al-Hashmi told reporters: “The world is suffering enough with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, so we cannot also afford to add the Bab al-Mandab into that equation.” He added that the closure of the southern entrance to the Red Sea would be “catastrophic for the entire world … and we are already seeing the consequences”. The strait of Hormuz remained largely closed for commercial traffic on Monday and Tuesday, with a Qatar ship disabled by Iran and only four ships recorded as crossing the strait on Monday compared with a prewar average of about 130 ships. So far Donald Trump has rejected Saudi pleas to join the fight to drive the Houthis back north up the coast of the Red Sea. Houthi leaders have also spoken to the US vice-president, JD Vance, reassuring the White House that their forces are seeking only to hinder Saudi-owned shipping, and that their overall goal is to end what they regard as a Saudi blockade of Houthi-controlled areas. The Houthis have signed a ceasefire agreement with the US, but are still subject to US sanctions. The UK is unlikely to offer direct military, as opposed to political, support to Saudi Arabia unless there is a clear instruction from Washington to do so. Inside Yemen the next military engagement is likely to focus on the city of Marib where Saudi air raids have been trying to weaken Houthi formations. Yemen’s ministry of foreign affairs and expatriates said: “If the world wants stability and calm in the region, it must tell the Saudis: enough interference in the Yemeni affair.” Rather than giving direct military help, western governments are providing intelligence, including targeting advice as well as strategic help in the task of trying to integrate the disparate anti-Houthi forces in Yemen. A map of Yemen annotated with details of locations of military actions that have taken place in September 2026. Houthi forces have been advancing in recent days amid a new offensive. But Maysaa Shuja al-Deen from the Sana’a Center thinktank said: “Any renewed military campaign must be accompanied by a serious reassessment of past mistakes, meaningful reform of the Yemeni government, stronger coordination among anti-Houthi forces, and a more balanced relationship between Yemeni actors and their regional partners.” She added: “In many cases, the Saudis choose Yemeni figures who are weak, easily manipulated, and willing to follow their orders. If they instead chose competent, strong actors who could implement a shared agenda, they would also gain the respect of other competent Yemeni figures. “This approach contrasts with the Iranian and Emirati models, which have generally given their local allies more room to manoeuvre while building relationships around specific objectives and clearer mandates.” Due to the weakness of the UN-recognised government in Yemen, various militias with different ideological or regional loyalties operate alongside the official national army. Together on paper, the number of anti-Houthi forces could reach as many as 500,000 troops but in practice not all these forces cooperate or are willing to fight outside their area. Saudi Arabia gives support to Yemen’s Homeland Shield Forces while the United Arab Emirates had backed both the 80,000-strong Southern Transitional Council’s Giants Brigade and a 20,000-strong force led by Tareq Saleh. But the UAE, after backing separatist forces in the south, has now pulled out of Yemen. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/liv.text: Good morning. We will be hearing from Andy Burnham today because he is back at work having taken time off following the death of his father. And already we have heard from Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, who has been doing a media round. She has condemned Elon Musk’s social media platform, X, describing it as an “absolute disgrace”. Nandy was talking about what social media companies are doing to stop people using their platforms to post intimidatory messages online, in particular posting private information like an address that might put someone at risk (doxxing). Yesterday Nandy hosted a meeting with social media companies about this, partly prompted by the abuse RNLI volunteers have been getting online by anti-migrant vigilantes who hate the lifeboat service for the role it plays protecting people on small boats at risk of drowning. Speaking on Times Radio this morning, Nandy said: I had the social media companies in to see me yesterday to talk to them about their responsibilitie

https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/10/17/leng.text: Menü Kereső Többezres tüntetést szervezett Donald Tusk ellen a PiS Varsóban Külföld Tüntetők 2026. október 17-én Varsóban a PiS által szervezett demonstráción – Fotó: Wojtek Radwanski / AFP Bánáti Anna Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Több ezer ember tüntetett szombat délután a varsói Alkotmánybíróság előtt az ellenzékben lévő Jog és Igazságosság (PiS) által összehívott demonstráción, írja a lengyel Gazeta Wyborcza . A párt politikusai az Alkotmánybíróság függetlenségéért és a lengyel értékek védelméért tüntettek. A megmozduláson a PiS-hez köthető Karol Nawrocki lengyel elnök nem jelent meg. Az MTI tudósítója szerint a tüntetés elején Jarosław Kaczyński, a korábban nyolc évig hatalmon lévő PiS elnöke arról beszélt, hogy meg kell védeni „a kormányzók által még el nem foglalt utolsó két intézmény” függetlenségét. Ezzel az alkotmánybíróságra és a jegybankra utalt. Felszólalt Pawel Szefernaker, az államfő kabinetfőnöke is, aki beszédében azzal vádolta Donald Tusk kormányát, hogy „teljes körű uralma alá akarja vonni” az alkotmánybíróságot és más független intézményeket. Az alkotmánybíróságnál már több napja tiltakoznak ellenzéki aktivisták, a tüntetők sátorvárost is építettek. A lengyel alkotmánybíróság 15 tagú, a szejm, a lengyel parlament alsóháza március óta nyolc új alkotmánybírót választott meg. Nawrocki hármat már beiktatott, a másik öt bíró eskütételéről egyelőre nem döntött, formális hiányosságokra hivatkozva. Donald Tusk szerdán arról beszélt, Nawrocki ezzel „lemondott az alkotmányos kötelességeinek teljesítéséről”. A 2023. októberi parlamenti választást a PiS nyerte Lengyelországban, de Kaczyński pártja messze volt a többségtől, nem tudott kormányt alakítani. Végül a Tusk mögött álló hármas szövetség kapott bizalmat a szejmben, és több területen is látványosan megpróbálták visszacsinálni a PiS lépéseit .
